solution:
Any equation of the form \(ax + by + c = 0\), where \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) are real numbers and \(a\), \(b\) are not both zero, is a linear equation in two variables. Five such equations are :
\(x + y = 5\); \(2x - y = 3\); \(3x + 4y = 12\); \(x - 5y + 7 = 0\); \(\dfrac{x}{2} + y = 4\)
(The answer is not unique — any five equations of this form are correct.)

Choose any value for \(x\) and find the matching \(y\) from \(y = 7 - x\).
\((0, 7)\), \((1, 6)\), \((2, 5)\), \((3, 4)\), \((7, 0)\)
Each pair satisfies \(x + y = 7\). (The answer is not unique — the equation has infinitely many solutions.)

\(x + y = 4\) ...(I); \(2x - 5y = 1\) ...(II)
Multiplying (I) by 5 : \(5x + 5y = 20\) ...(III)
Adding (II) and (III) : \(7x = 21\)
\(\therefore x = 3\)
Substituting in (I) : \(3 + y = 4\) \(\therefore y = 1\)
\(\therefore x = 3\); \(y = 1\)

\(2x + y = 5\) ...(I); \(3x - y = 5\) ...(II)
Adding (I) and (II) : \(5x = 10\)
\(\therefore x = 2\)
Substituting in (I) : \(4 + y = 5\) \(\therefore y = 1\)
\(\therefore x = 2\); \(y = 1\)

\(2y - x = 0\) ...(I); \(10x + 15y = 105\) ...(II)
From (I), \(x = 2y\). Substituting in (II) :
\(10(2y) + 15y = 105\)
\(35y = 105\) \(\therefore y = 3\)
\(\therefore x = 2 \times 3 = 6\)
\(\therefore x = 6\); \(y = 3\)

[Textbook misprint: as printed, "Number of 5 rupee notes are less by 10 than number of 10 rupee notes" gives \(15y = 400\), i.e. a non-whole number of notes, so the question has no valid answer. The book's own printed answer (30 notes of 5 and 20 notes of 10) requires the opposite direction — the number of TEN rupee notes is less by 10 than the number of FIVE rupee notes. The stem is preserved as printed and the model answer works through both readings.]

Let the number of 5 rupee notes be \(x\) and the number of 10 rupee notes be \(y\).
Total amount : \(5x + 10y = 350\) ...(I)
As printed, "number of 5 rupee notes are less by 10 than number of 10 rupee notes" gives \(x = y - 10\) ...(II)
Substituting (II) in (I) : \(5(y - 10) + 10y = 350\)
\(15y = 400\) \(\therefore y = \dfrac{80}{3}\), which is not a whole number — so as printed the question has no valid answer.
Reading the condition the other way round, i.e. the number of 10 rupee notes is less by 10 than the number of 5 rupee notes (\(y = x - 10\)) :
\(5x + 10(x - 10) = 350\)
\(15x = 450\) \(\therefore x = 30\), and \(y = 20\)
\(\therefore\) there are 30 five-rupee notes and 20 ten-rupee notes, which is the answer the textbook prints. Check : \(5 \times 30 + 10 \times 20 = 150 + 200 = 350\).

Let the numerator be \(x\) and the denominator be \(y\).
The denominator is 1 less than twice the numerator : \(y = 2x - 1\) ...(I)
Adding 1 to each : \(\dfrac{x + 1}{y + 1} = \dfrac{3}{5}\) \(\therefore 5(x + 1) = 3(y + 1)\)
\(\therefore 5x + 5 = 3y + 3\) \(\therefore 5x - 3y = -2\) ...(II)
Substituting (I) in (II) : \(5x - 3(2x - 1) = -2\)
\(5x - 6x + 3 = -2\) \(\therefore -x = -5\) \(\therefore x = 5\)
\(\therefore y = 2(5) - 1 = 9\)
\(\therefore\) the fraction is \(\dfrac{5}{9}\).

Let Priyanka's age be \(x\) years and Deepika's age be \(y\) years.
\(x + y = 34\) ...(I)
\(x - y = 6\) ...(II)
Adding (I) and (II) : \(2x = 40\) \(\therefore x = 20\)
Substituting in (I) : \(20 + y = 34\) \(\therefore y = 14\)
\(\therefore\) Priyanka's age is 20 years and Deepika's age is 14 years.

Let the number of lions be \(x\) and the number of peacocks be \(y\).
\(x + y = 50\) ...(I)
A lion has 4 legs and a peacock has 2 legs : \(4x + 2y = 140\) ...(II)
Multiplying (I) by 2 : \(2x + 2y = 100\) ...(III)
Subtracting (III) from (II) : \(2x = 40\) \(\therefore x = 20\)
\(\therefore y = 50 - 20 = 30\)
\(\therefore\) there are 20 lions and 30 peacocks.

Let the original monthly salary be \(x\) rupees and the yearly increment be \(y\) rupees.
After 4 years : \(x + 4y = 4500\) ...(I)
After 10 years : \(x + 10y = 5400\) ...(II)
Subtracting (I) from (II) : \(6y = 900\) \(\therefore y = 150\)
Substituting in (I) : \(x + 600 = 4500\) \(\therefore x = 3900\)
\(\therefore\) the initial salary is 3900 rupees and the yearly increment is 150 rupees.

Let the price of one chair be \(x\) rupees and of one table be \(y\) rupees.
\(3x + 2y = 4500\) ...(I)
\(5x + 3y = 7000\) ...(II)
Multiplying (I) by 3 and (II) by 2 :
\(9x + 6y = 13500\) ...(III)
\(10x + 6y = 14000\) ...(IV)
Subtracting (III) from (IV) : \(x = 500\)
Substituting in (I) : \(1500 + 2y = 4500\) \(\therefore y = 1500\)
Price of 2 chairs and 2 tables \(= 2(500) + 2(1500) = 1000 + 3000\)
\(\therefore\) the total price is 4000 rupees.

Let the tens place digit be \(x\) and the units place digit be \(y\).
Sum of the digits : \(x + y = 9\) ...(I)
The original number is \(10x + y\); interchanging gives \(10y + x\).
\((10y + x) - (10x + y) = 27\)
\(9y - 9x = 27\) \(\therefore y - x = 3\) ...(II)
Adding (I) and (II) : \(2y = 12\) \(\therefore y = 6\)
\(\therefore x = 9 - 6 = 3\)
\(\therefore\) the two-digit number is \(10(3) + 6 = 36\).

Let \(\angle B = x\) and \(\angle C = y\).
\(\angle A = \angle B + \angle C = x + y\)
The sum of the angles of a triangle is \(180^\circ\) :
\((x + y) + x + y = 180\) \(\therefore 2(x + y) = 180\) \(\therefore x + y = 90\) ...(I)
\(\therefore \angle A = 90^\circ\)
The ratio of \(\angle B\) to \(\angle C\) is \(4 : 5\), so \(x = 4k\) and \(y = 5k\).
\(4k + 5k = 90\) \(\therefore 9k = 90\) \(\therefore k = 10\)
\(\therefore \angle B = 40^\circ\) and \(\angle C = 50^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle A = 90^\circ\), \(\angle B = 40^\circ\), \(\angle C = 50^\circ\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives 420 cm for the larger part. With the smaller part 140 cm and the larger 420 cm, twice the smaller is 280 while one-third of the larger is 140 — the stated condition fails. Solving \(x + y = 560\) with \(2x = \tfrac{y}{3}\) gives smaller 80 cm and larger 480 cm, and then \(2 \times 80 = 160 = \tfrac{1}{3} \times 480\). The key's 420 answers a different condition (twice the smaller \(=\) two-thirds of the larger).]

Let the smaller part be \(x\) cm and the larger part be \(y\) cm.
\(x + y = 560\) ...(I)
Twice the smaller part equals \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) of the larger part : \(2x = \dfrac{y}{3}\) \(\therefore y = 6x\) ...(II)
Substituting (II) in (I) : \(x + 6x = 560\)
\(7x = 560\) \(\therefore x = 80\)
\(\therefore y = 6 \times 80 = 480\)
\(\therefore\) the length of the larger part is 480 cm.
Check : the smaller part is 80 cm, \(2 \times 80 = 160\), and \(\dfrac{1}{3} \times 480 = 160\). The two are equal, as required.

Let the number of correct answers be \(x\) and the number of wrong answers be \(y\).
All 60 questions were attempted : \(x + y = 60\) ...(I)
Marks : \(2x - y = 90\) ...(II)
Adding (I) and (II) : \(3x = 150\) \(\therefore x = 50\)
\(\therefore y = 60 - 50 = 10\)
\(\therefore\) he got 10 questions wrong.

\(2x + y = 5\) ...(I); \(3x - y = 5\) ...(II)
Adding : \(5x = 10\) \(\therefore x = 2\)
Substituting in (I) : \(4 + y = 5\) \(\therefore y = 1\)
\(\therefore x = 2\); \(y = 1\)

\(x - 2y = -1\) ...(I); \(2x - y = 7\) ...(II)
From (I), \(x = 2y - 1\). Substituting in (II) :
\(2(2y - 1) - y = 7\) \(\therefore 3y = 9\) \(\therefore y = 3\)
\(\therefore x = 2(3) - 1 = 5\)
\(\therefore x = 5\); \(y = 3\)

\(x + y = 11\) ...(I); \(2x - 3y = 7\) ...(II)
From (I), \(x = 11 - y\). Substituting in (II) :
\(2(11 - y) - 3y = 7\) \(\therefore 22 - 5y = 7\) \(\therefore 5y = 15\) \(\therefore y = 3\)
\(\therefore x = 11 - 3 = 8\)
\(\therefore x = 8\); \(y = 3\)

\(2x + y = -2\) ...(I); \(3x - y = 7\) ...(II)
Adding : \(5x = 5\) \(\therefore x = 1\)
Substituting in (I) : \(2 + y = -2\) \(\therefore y = -4\)
\(\therefore x = 1\); \(y = -4\)

\(2x - y = 5\) ...(I); \(3x + 2y = 11\) ...(II)
Multiplying (I) by 2 : \(4x - 2y = 10\) ...(III)
Adding (II) and (III) : \(7x = 21\) \(\therefore x = 3\)
Substituting in (I) : \(6 - y = 5\) \(\therefore y = 1\)
\(\therefore x = 3\); \(y = 1\)

\(x - 2y = -2\) ...(I); \(x + 2y = 10\) ...(II)
Adding : \(2x = 8\) \(\therefore x = 4\)
Substituting in (II) : \(4 + 2y = 10\) \(\therefore y = 3\)
\(\therefore x = 4\); \(y = 3\)

\(3x - 4y = 7\) ...(I); \(5x + 2y = 3\) ...(II)
To equate the coefficients of \(y\), multiply (II) by 2 : \(10x + 4y = 6\) ...(III)
Adding (I) and (III) : \(13x = 13\) \(\therefore x = 1\)
Substituting in (I) : \(3 - 4y = 7\) \(\therefore -4y = 4\) \(\therefore y = -1\)
\(\therefore x = 1\); \(y = -1\)

\(5x + 7y = 17\) ...(I); \(3x - 2y = 4\) ...(II)
Multiplying (I) by 2 and (II) by 7 :
\(10x + 14y = 34\) ...(III)
\(21x - 14y = 28\) ...(IV)
Adding (III) and (IV) : \(31x = 62\) \(\therefore x = 2\)
Substituting in (II) : \(6 - 2y = 4\) \(\therefore y = 1\)
\(\therefore x = 2\); \(y = 1\)

\(x - 2y = -10\) ...(I); \(3x - 5y = -12\) ...(II)
Multiplying (I) by 3 : \(3x - 6y = -30\) ...(III)
Subtracting (III) from (II) : \(y = 18\)
Substituting in (I) : \(x - 36 = -10\) \(\therefore x = 26\)
\(\therefore x = 26\); \(y = 18\)

\(4x + y = 34\) ...(I); \(x + 4y = 16\) ...(II)
Multiplying (I) by 4 : \(16x + 4y = 136\) ...(III)
Subtracting (II) from (III) : \(15x = 120\) \(\therefore x = 8\)
Substituting in (I) : \(32 + y = 34\) \(\therefore y = 2\)
\(\therefore x = 8\); \(y = 2\)

\(\dfrac{x}{3} + \dfrac{y}{4} = 4\). Multiplying by 12 : \(4x + 3y = 48\) ...(I)
\(\dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{y}{4} = 1\). Multiplying by 4 : \(2x - y = 4\) ...(II)
Multiplying (II) by 3 : \(6x - 3y = 12\) ...(III)
Adding (I) and (III) : \(10x = 60\) \(\therefore x = 6\)
Substituting in (II) : \(12 - y = 4\) \(\therefore y = 8\)
\(\therefore x = 6\); \(y = 8\)

\(\dfrac{x}{3} + 5y = 13\). Multiplying by 3 : \(x + 15y = 39\) ...(I)
\(2x + \dfrac{y}{2} = 19\). Multiplying by 2 : \(4x + y = 38\) ...(II)
From (II), \(y = 38 - 4x\). Substituting in (I) :
\(x + 15(38 - 4x) = 39\) \(\therefore x + 570 - 60x = 39\)
\(-59x = -531\) \(\therefore x = 9\)
\(\therefore y = 38 - 36 = 2\)
\(\therefore x = 9\); \(y = 2\)

Put \(\dfrac{1}{x} = p\) and \(\dfrac{1}{y} = q\). The equations become
\(2p + 3q = 13\) ...(I)
\(5p - 4q = -2\) ...(II)
Multiplying (I) by 4 and (II) by 3 :
\(8p + 12q = 52\) ...(III)
\(15p - 12q = -6\) ...(IV)
Adding (III) and (IV) : \(23p = 46\) \(\therefore p = 2\)
Substituting in (I) : \(4 + 3q = 13\) \(\therefore q = 3\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{x} = 2\) and \(\dfrac{1}{y} = 3\)
\(\therefore x = \dfrac{1}{2}\); \(y = \dfrac{1}{3}\)

Let the tens place digit be \(x\) and the units place digit be \(y\), so the number is \(10x + y\).
The number is 3 more than 4 times the sum of its digits :
\(10x + y = 4(x + y) + 3\) \(\therefore 6x - 3y = 3\) \(\therefore 2x - y = 1\) ...(I)
Adding 18 gives the number with digits interchanged :
\(10x + y + 18 = 10y + x\) \(\therefore 9x - 9y = -18\) \(\therefore x - y = -2\) ...(II)
Subtracting (II) from (I) : \(x = 3\)
Substituting in (II) : \(3 - y = -2\) \(\therefore y = 5\)
\(\therefore\) the number is \(10(3) + 5 = 35\).

Let the cost of one book be \(x\) rupees and of one pen be \(y\) rupees.
\(8x + 5y = 420\) ...(I)
\(5x + 8y = 321\) ...(II)
Adding (I) and (II) : \(13x + 13y = 741\) \(\therefore x + y = 57\) ...(III)
Subtracting (II) from (I) : \(3x - 3y = 99\) \(\therefore x - y = 33\) ...(IV)
Adding (III) and (IV) : \(2x = 90\) \(\therefore x = 45\)
\(\therefore y = 57 - 45 = 12\)
Cost of 1 book and 2 pens \(= 45 + 2(12) = 45 + 24\)
\(\therefore\) the cost is 69 rupees.

Let the incomes be \(9k\) and \(7k\), and the expenses be \(4m\) and \(3m\).
Savings = income \(-\) expense, and each saves 200 :
\(9k - 4m = 200\) ...(I)
\(7k - 3m = 200\) ...(II)
Multiplying (I) by 3 and (II) by 4 :
\(27k - 12m = 600\) ...(III)
\(28k - 12m = 800\) ...(IV)
Subtracting (III) from (IV) : \(k = 200\)
\(\therefore\) the incomes are \(9 \times 200 = 1800\) rupees and \(7 \times 200 = 1400\) rupees.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives length 347 and breadth 207. Those satisfy the second condition (\(344 \times 209 = 71896 = 71829 + 67\)) but NOT the first: \(342 \times 210 = 71820\), which is 9 less than \(347 \times 207 = 71829\), where the question requires a reduction of 8. Solving \(3x - 5y = 7\) and \(2x - 3y = 73\) gives length 344 and breadth 205, which satisfies both conditions exactly.]

Let the length be \(x\) units and the breadth be \(y\) units, so the area is \(xy\).
First condition : \((x - 5)(y + 3) = xy - 8\)
\(xy + 3x - 5y - 15 = xy - 8\) \(\therefore 3x - 5y = 7\) ...(I)
Second condition : \((x - 3)(y + 2) = xy + 67\)
\(xy + 2x - 3y - 6 = xy + 67\) \(\therefore 2x - 3y = 73\) ...(II)
Multiplying (I) by 3 and (II) by 5 :
\(9x - 15y = 21\) ...(III)
\(10x - 15y = 365\) ...(IV)
Subtracting (III) from (IV) : \(x = 344\)
Substituting in (II) : \(688 - 3y = 73\) \(\therefore 3y = 615\) \(\therefore y = 205\)
\(\therefore\) the length is 344 units and the breadth is 205 units.
Check : area \(= 344 \times 205 = 70520\); \(339 \times 208 = 70512 = 70520 - 8\) and \(341 \times 207 = 70587 = 70520 + 67\). Both conditions hold.

Let the speeds of the two cars be \(x\) km/hr and \(y\) km/hr, with \(x > y\).
Travelling in the same direction the gap of 70 km closes in 7 hours :
\(7(x - y) = 70\) \(\therefore x - y = 10\) ...(I)
Travelling towards each other they cover 70 km in 1 hour :
\(x + y = 70\) ...(II)
Adding (I) and (II) : \(2x = 80\) \(\therefore x = 40\)
\(\therefore y = 70 - 40 = 30\)
\(\therefore\) the speeds are 40 km/hr and 30 km/hr.

Let the tens place digit be \(x\) and the units place digit be \(y\).
The number is \(10x + y\) and the interchanged number is \(10y + x\).
\((10x + y) + (10y + x) = 99\)
\(11x + 11y = 99\) \(\therefore x + y = 9\)
So ANY two-digit number whose digits add up to 9 satisfies the condition.
\(\therefore\) the number can be 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72, 81 or 90 (and the corresponding interchanged numbers). For example, \(54 + 45 = 99\) and \(36 + 63 = 99\).
